title: At a large public university system, high-school grades predict academic success better than standardized tests
source_unit: NBER Working Paper 34975 administrative-data study of a large urban public university system
geography: United States; large urban public university system and first-year cohorts entering 2010–2019

denominator.unit: first-year student cohorts in a large urban public university system; public abstract does not disclose the full sample count

predictive_ranking.value: high-school GPA is the dominant predictor of first-year academic outcomes and graduation rates in the studied public system
predictive_ranking.unit: relative predictive performance of admissions measures

sat_comparison.value: re-establishing an SAT requirement would not necessarily improve predictability in this public-university context

context_contrast.value: the result contrasts with recent evidence from Ivy-Plus institutions where standardized tests predict college success more strongly than high-school GPA

observations.method: Analysis of administrative data for 2010–2019 first-year cohorts, comparing the predictive power of high-school GPA and SAT scores for first-year outcomes and graduation rates.
observations.uncertainty: The public abstract does not disclose the full sample count, all outcome definitions, subgroup estimates, or whether changing an admissions requirement would change access, preparation, or later earnings.
observations.subgroup: Students entering a large urban public university system; comparison context includes Ivy-Plus institutions but is not a pooled estimate.
observations.counterinterpretation: High-school GPA may capture sustained performance and school context rather than pure academic preparation; a predictive measure can still have distributional, coaching, or access effects, and test-optional policy may alter who submits scores.

related_sources.claim: NBER DOI record for the working paper.
Official working-paper PDF for administrative-data and predictive-validity details.

boundary: This record compares predictive validity in one public-university system and a separate elite-institution context. It does not establish an admissions reform effect, access or inequality effect, student wellbeing, degree completion causality, earnings, or public trust.
